comment.value: This paper proposes PoET-2, a multimodal, retrieval-augmented protein foundation model with a dual-decoder design that integrates sequence and structural context for variant effect prediction. The model demonstrates clear strengths: it uniquely enables zero-shot prediction of indels and higher-order variants, achieves strong data efficiency in supervised settings, provides high-quality embeddings for downstream tasks, and is competitive with much larger models while showing complementarity with VenusREM through ensembling. Weaknesses include underperformance on standard substitution benchmarks without ensembling, reliance on homolog/structure retrieval which may limit use cases for orphan proteins, and some lack of clarity on application scenarios where PoET-2 outperforms existing models. Overall, given its novel contributions in indel prediction and efficiency, I recommend acceptance.

author_final_remarks.value:
We thank the reviewers for their insightful feedback and constructive engagement, which has helped us to improve the manuscript.

We propose PoET-2, a retrieval-augmentated, multimodal protein foundation model, which infers family-specific evolutionary constraints from sequences and optional structures at inference time. Its novel dual-decoder design addresses current generative and representation learning limitations. Structure-aware PLMs are SOTA for zero-shot substitution variant effect prediction, but cannot predict indel effects and poorly model high order mutations. Our autoregressive decoder and context encoding architecture enables zero-shot prediction of indel effects with structures for the first time. However, autoregressive models are not ideal for representation learning due to their lack of bidirectionality. Therefore, we introduce a bidirectional decoder which generates rich vector embeddings for downstream tasks.

As the reviewers have highlighted, PoET2 demonstrates impact in two key areas:

* **Supervised prediction:** PoET-2 **outperforms previous SOTA models** on mutation function prediction benchmarks. PoET-2 also achieves an order-of-magnitude improvement in data efficiency, achieving previous SOTA with 2-30x less data. This is crucial for protein ML on small, real-world experimental datasets.  
    
* **Zero-shot:** PoET-2 establishes a new SOTA for predicting the effects of indels in DMS assays and clinical variants. It is the **only structure-aware model capable of scoring indels**, overcoming a significant limitation of prior models. For substitutions in DMS assays, it delivers strong performance on par with top existing methods. 

The primary discussion otherwise revolved around the ProteinGym substitution DMS analysis benchmark and comparison with VenusREM. We have now addressed the main concerns of the reviewers by more clearly contextualizing the performance of PoET-2 and the PoET-2+VenusREM ensemble. We note that this result is scientifically interesting because it suggests that PoET-2 may be capturing orthogonal information to the existing VenusREM ensemble. We have also improved the final manuscript to better articulate these results. 

Overall, our results demonstrate that PoET-2 widely applies to supervised and zero-shot tasks, providing a strong and efficient foundation model for diverse protein ML challenges, and suggest new directions for parameter efficient protein language models.

Thank you for your response. We would like to emphasize that zero-shot prediction of substitution effects in DMS assays is just one of many tasks we benchmark PoET-2 on. We also show that PoET-2 is state-of-the-art across a broader set of representation learning and zero-shot benchmarks, including supervised prediction, and zero-shot prediction of indels and clinical variants. PoET-2 is remarkable given its ability to perform well across all of these settings, in contrast to other models in the field.

- For **supervised** prediction, PoET-2 (1) significantly outperforms prior state-of-the-art models when trained on the same amount of data, and (2) requires an order of magnitude less data to match the state-of-the-art. This enables protein engineering with significantly lower throughput assays and/or cost.
- For **zero-shot** prediction, PoET-2 achieves state-of-the-art performance on DMS indels and clinical variant effect prediction (both substitutions and indels). In particular, PoET-2 is able to accurately score indel variants, overcoming a key limitation of prior structure-aware methods such as VenusREM. We discuss the significance of modeling indels in our rebuttal.

Zero-shot substitution variant effect prediction is just one task and PoET-2's high performance and complementarity with VenusREM still suggests interesting future directions in regards to saturation of this task. We hope the reviewer will consider this contribution holistically, as our contribution with PoET-2 is much more than just zero-shot DMS substitution prediction. PoET-2 is unique in its ability to perform well in a wide range of tasks, thanks to its architectural design.

rebuttal.value:
Thank you for your insightful comments and questions. We address each of your comments below, and hope that our answers and proposed adjustments to the manuscript clarify the significance of our work.

> W1: Structure Conditioning Limitations: Shows limited improvement for clinical and supervised prediction tasks.

Although structure conditioning is not helpful for some tasks, we show that it significantly improves performance in other tasks, such as zero-shot variant effect prediction of substitutions. Therefore, structure conditioning remains a critical component of our method. It is expected that structure conditioning is more helpful in some tasks, such as predicting protein stability, and less helpful in other tasks, such as predicting organismal fitness, where there are more factors influencing protein fitness than just structure. Thus, limited improvement in some tasks may also reflect the nature of the task itself.

> W2: Lack of Public Code: The paper states code and model weights will be released later, hindering immediate reproducibility.

To be more specific on the timeline, we will release code and models along with the paper.

> W3: Slight Underperformance on DMS Stability Data: Slightly lags behind newer masked structure-based models in this specific setting.

Our results show that the performance of the best method presented in our paper for zero-shot variant effect of prediction of substitutions (the ensemble of PoET-2 and VenusREM) is comparable (i.e. within the margin of error) to existing state-of-the-art methods on DMS Stability Data (Appendix D.4 Table 10). It is important to recognize that the top performing baseline, VenusREM, is also an ensemble model. Specifically, VenusREM is an ensemble method that combines predictions from two models, ProSST (a structure-aware PLM) and PSSM (a model derived from MSAs) [1]. Therefore, for a fair comparison, VenusREM should be compared to other model ensembles, such as our proposed ensemble of PoET-2 and VenusREM. We find that ensembling PoET-2 and VenusREM significantly outperforms either method alone for zero-shot variant effect prediction of substitutions (Table 1), and matches or exceeds the performance of either method alone across all subcategories studied, including different assay types, MSA depths, taxonomies, and mutation depths (Appendix D.4 Tables 10-13). To clarify the importance of ensembling for future readers, in our final manuscript, we will (1) add an explanation of VenusREM's use of ensembling, and (2) discuss the importance of ensembling as a general technique for zero-shot variant effect prediction.

Furthermore, we have observed that ensembling PoET-2 and ProSST performs identically to ensembling PoET-2 and VenusREM. This simplified model ensemble significantly advances the state-of-the-art for zero-shot variant effect prediction of substitutions while ensembling the same number of models as VenusREM.

Lastly, the observation that ensembling PoET-2 with ProSST (or VenusREM) significantly outperforms either method alone also has significant scientific value. It indicates that the two methods capture orthogonal aspects of protein function, and suggests that future methods can combine aspects of both individual methods in a more complex manner to further advance our ability to make zero-shot predictions, particularly for indels which are not supported by ProSST/VenusREM. We look forward to future work exploring this possibility.

> Q1: How does PoET-2 balance between structure-aware modeling and data availability when predicted structures are missing or low confidence?

PoET-2 is designed to be robust to missing and/or low confidence structures.

1. We find that in tasks where using structure inputs is helpful, PoET-2 retains the majority of its performance even if structures are not used (Appendix D, Table 5). 
2. If predicted structures are missing, they can always be manually predicted using high quality open source tools such as AlphaFold2 or Boltz-2, although doing so increases the computational cost of using PoET-2. In practice, the existence of large predicted structure databases such as AlphaFoldDB and ESM Metagenomic Atlas mean that predicted structures are readily available for many proteins of interest. 
3. In order to handle low confidence structures, PoET-2 adopts two main strategies. First, PoET-2 uses the predicted confidence at each residue (pLDDT), as an input to the model (lines 158-160). This makes PoET-2 directly aware of which positions are predicted with lower confidence. Second, PoET-2 does not use structure information at low confidence residues where pLDDT < 70 (line 172). This ensures that PoET-2 is not biased by erroneous structure predictions.

> Q2: How sensitive is the model to the number and diversity of homologs provided during prompting?

PoET-2 performs well even with few homologs, though as expected, it performs better when there are more homologs available. Table 1 shows the performance of PoET-2 and baseline models broken down by availability of homologs, as measured by the "MSA Depth" metric defined in the ProteinGym benchmark [2]. PoET-2 performs well in all three MSA Depth categories (Low, Medium, High). PoET-2 outperforms all non-ensemble baselines in the Low MSA Depth category, and is within the margin of error compared to the top ensemble baseline, VenusREM (Appendix Table 11). Additionally, the ensemble of PoET-2 and VenusREM outperforms either method alone across all MSA Depths.

Another way to view your question is from the perspective of artificially limiting the number of homologs used in the prompt, even when more homologs are available. We observe the same trends for PoET-2 as was observed for PoET-1 [3, Appendix D] . Specifically, the model performs best with a modest context length of 6000-12000 tokens, although there is significant variation between assays.

> Q3: Are there specific protein families where PoET-2 underperforms, and why?

In our analysis, we did not identify any protein families where PoET-2 systematically underperforms relative to other models. Generally, we find that performance across different models is highly correlated. Therefore, we believe that protein families where all models perform poorly are likely those where the assayed function is not a strong driver of evolution.

> Q4: How does PoET-2 perform in real-world protein engineering campaigns compared to baseline PLMs?

PoET-2's excellent performance in benchmarks, which cover a wide variety of proteins, protein functions, and use cases (DMS and clinical data, substitution and indel variants, higher-order-mutants, zero-shot and few-shot/supervised settings), indicates that it would outperform baseline PLMs in real-world protein engineering across a wide range of tasks. We plan to publish experimental results of protein engineering campaigns using PoET-2 in the future.

> L1: Structure information contributes selectively to task performance, being more useful for stability prediction than functional classification.

Please refer to our response to W1 above.

> L2: Although designed for few-shot learning, performance might still vary with extremely sparse data.

We agree that performance on extremely sparse data is a key test. To provide rigorous support for our claims in this regime, we performed a bootstrap analysis (10,000 samples) to compute the statistical significance of PoET-2's performance advantage.

Table B below focuses on the few-shot setting where only `n=10` training datapoints are available. It shows that PoET-2 consistently outperforms all baselines by a large and statistically significant margin. All differences in Table B are significant with $p<4.5e-3$. This trend holds across all dataset sizes studied, with p-values for `n>10` being even more significant, with $p<1e-5$. These data confirm our results are robust and not an artifact of data sparsity. We will add this analysis to the final manuscript.

> L3: The model relies on precomputed homologs and structures, potentially limiting use cases with novel or uncharacterized proteins.

Please refer to our response to Q2 above.

> L4: Current benchmarks may not fully represent in vivo protein function complexity.

While the benchmarks may not cover every aspect of protein function, they have substantial coverage, covering in vitro and in vivo aspects of protein function across hundreds of proteins in DMS assays, and the variant effects of thousands of clinically relevant proteins. Overall, VenusREM still appears to be a stronger tool for protein engineering.

Our results show that PoET-2 and VenusREM are highly complementary for protein engineering - where applicable, combining the models via ensembling significantly outperforms either method alone. To obtain the best zero-shot variant effect predictions for substitutions, practitioners should use the ensemble of the two models and *not VenusREM alone*. The use of ensembling should not be considered a weakness of our method relative to baselines because it is a technique used by many baselines, including VenusREM. To clarify the importance of ensembling for future readers, in our final manuscript, we will (1) add an explanation of VenusREM's use of ensembling, and (2) discuss the importance of ensembling as a general technique for zero-shot variant effect prediction.

Ensembling techniques employed by both baselines and our proposed methods include:

1. Ensembling over prompts: Both the MSA Transformer and PoET-1 baselines ensemble over prompts by conditioning on different subsamples of homologs from an MSA [1,2].
2. Ensembling different model types: The VenusREM baseline is an ensemble model that combines predictions from two different models by taking a weighted average of the scores from each individual model [3]. These two models are (1) ProSST, a structure-aware PLM, and (2) PSSM, a model derived from MSAs. The ensemble of PoET-2 and VenusREM presented in our paper employs this technique to combine predictions from PoET-2 and VenusREM, and it establishes a new state-of-the-art.

Furthermore, we have observed that ensembling PoET-2 and ProSST performs identically to ensembling PoET-2 and VenusREM. This simplified model ensemble significantly advances the state-of-the-art while ensembling the same number of models as VenusREM.

The observation that ensembling PoET-2 with ProSST (or VenusREM) significantly outperforms either method alone also has significant scientific value. It indicates that the two methods capture orthogonal aspects of protein function, and suggests that future methods can combine aspects of both individual methods in a more complex manner to further advance our ability to make zero-shot predictions, particularly for indels which are not supported by ProSST/VenusREM. We look forward to future work exploring this possibility.

> Q1: Since the pairwise distances between backbone atoms are already given, the position of each $C_\alpha$ atom is mostly determined. Is the additional local distance feature $x_{atomb}$ really necessary? Is there any ablation study to show its impact?

The purpose of the additional local distance feature is to capture information about the backbone (N, Ca, and C atoms) that is not included in the pairwise distances between just the Ca atoms. For example, the secondary structure depends on the positions of the N and C atoms, cannot be fully recovered from the pairwise distances of Ca atoms. In early experiments, we found that the local distance feature had minimal impact on the benchmarks presented in this paper. Nevertheless, we kept this feature to ensure the model has access to more complete information about the protein backbone. We will add this justification to the final manuscript.

> Q2: For the retrieval step, the model only uses AlphaFoldDB structures corresponding to the query sequences. These predicted structures may be low-quality in some cases. Could the authors consider using a template search strategy, similar to AlphaFold's, to improve retrieval quality?

We have not explored using experimental PDB structures like AlphaFold, but we think this would be a promising line of future work. Previous work suggests that to achieve optimal performance when using PDB structures, it may be helpful to include PDB structures, rather than just AFDB structures, during pre-training [4]. This may also be true for PoET-2; the current iteration of PoET-2 is only trained using AFDB structures.

Are there specific settings where PoET-2 clearly outperforms VenusREM on its own, without relying on model ensembling?

Given that VenusREM is itself an ensemble model, for fair comparison, VenusREM should be compared to other model ensembles, such as the ensemble of PoET-2 and VenusREM (or ProSST); see the response to W1 above for more information. The comprehensive benchmark results presented in our paper strongly support the conclusion that PoET-2 should be utilized in all of the protein engineering applications studied. The benchmarks cover hundreds of proteins and protein functions from DMS assay data, and thousands of clinically relevant proteins. - for zero-shot variant effect prediction of substitutions, the ensemble of PoET-2 and VenusREM (or ProSST) should be employed as it performs significantly better on the benchmark than all other methods (Table 1).
- for zero-shot variant effect prediction of indels, PoET-2 should be employed as it performs significantly better on the benchmark than all other methods (Table 1). - viral proteins (Appendix Table 12)

We will revise Section 3 of the main text to reference the additional methods detailed in Appendix B.5 to ensure that readers are aware of the additional methods. The methods currently described in Section 3 correspond to aspects of the model architecture and design that are directly utilized for the experimental results in the following sections; they are the aspects of the model that are most critical for the reader to understand. On the other hand, the additional features of the model described in Appendix B.5 are not directly utilized for the experimental results, and are less critical for understanding the contributions described in the main text.

> W3: Figure 1 lacks a caption and is not straightforward to understand without one. For example, what exactly are the outputs of PoET-2?

The outputs of PoET-2 used in the benchmarks are the sequence log-likelihoods from the autoregressive decoder, and the embeddings from the bidirectional decoder. We will add a more comprehensive caption to Figure 1 in the final manuscript.

We agree that the term "protein function" is somewhat ambiguous, as it can take on different meanings in different contexts. In our view, protein function and protein fitness are directly related, as protein fitness generally refers to a specific measure of protein function. For example, the ProteinGym paper [1] uses the following definition of protein fitness: "The protein fitness landscape refers to the mapping between genotype (e.g., the amino acid sequence) and phenotype (e.g., protein function)." For the final manuscript, we will conduct a thorough literature review to identify which term, fitness or function, is more commonly used to refer to the tasks described in the paper, and adjust the title accordingly.

> C2: The title, abstract, and introduction mention “retrieval-augmented,” but afterwards this concept is only mentioned in the discussion and not in the methods section. Please clarify what is meant by “retrieval-augmented.” Does it refer to the model’s ability to retrieve MSA sequences given a query sequences?

Yes, it refers to PoET-2's ability to condition on homologs (which typically come from an MSA). We will refine the manuscript to explictly define "retrieval-augmented" in the methods section.

> C3: Please discuss VenusREM in related work and describe the ensembling procedure.

The methodological details of VenusREM, in particular its use of ensembling, is important context for our work, and we will add a discussion of it to related work. Specifically, the VenusREM baseline is an ensemble model that combines predictions from two different models by taking a weighted average of the scores from each individual model [2]. These two models are (1) ProSST, a structure-aware PLM, and (2) PSSM, a model derived from MSAs. The ensemble of PoET-2 and VenusREM presented in our paper also employs this ensembling method to combine predictions from PoET-2 and VenusREM, and the ensembling method is fully detailed in Appendix D.3.

Furthermore, we have observed that ensembling PoET-2 and ProSST performs identically to ensembling PoET-2 and VenusREM. This simplified model ensemble significantly advances the state-of-the-art for zero-shot variant effect prediction of substitutions while ensembling the same number of models as VenusREM.

The observation that ensembling PoET-2 with ProSST (or VenusREM) significantly outperforms either method alone also has significant scientific value. It indicates that the two methods capture orthogonal aspects of protein function, and suggests that future methods can combine aspects of both individual methods in a more complex manner to further advance our ability to make zero-shot predictions, particularly for indels which are not supported by ProSST/VenusREM. We look forward to future work exploring this possibility.

For reference, lines 130-132 relate to PoET-2's bidirectional (MLM) decoder embeddings, and state: "These rich representations capture deep structural and functional insights, crucial for tasks like structure and function prediction where understanding global dependencies is key."

Unlike the MLM decoder, which produces an embedding for each residue that is a function of all residues, the CLM decoder produces an embedding for each residue that is only a function of the current and previous residues in the sequence. summary.value: The paper introduces PoET-2, a multimodal, retrieval-augmented protein foundation model designed to improve protein function prediction. Unlike prior PLMs, PoET-2 incorporates sequence and structural information from homologous proteins and leverages both causal and masked language modeling objectives. This allows it to operate in generative and bidirectional representation learning modes. PoET-2 shows state-of-the-art performance in zero-shot prediction of complex mutations (e.g., indels, higher-order mutations), clinical variant effect prediction, and few-shot supervised learning tasks. It achieves this with a modest 182M parameter footprint, demonstrating superior data efficiency and performance without requiring excessively large models.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
Strengths:

- Multimodality: Simultaneous use of sequence and structural data enhances the model’s understanding of protein function.

- Retrieval-Augmentation: Allows in-context learning from unaligned homologs, reducing reliance on massive parameter counts.

- Dual Decoders: Supports both generative and representation tasks, providing flexibility.

- State-of-the-Art Performance: Outperforms existing models on several benchmarks, especially in indel mutation and clinical variant effect prediction.

- Efficiency: Only 182M parameters yet comparable or superior to billion-scale models.

Weaknesses:

- Structure Conditioning Limitations: Shows limited improvement for clinical and supervised prediction tasks.


- Lack of Public Code: The paper states code and model weights will be released later, hindering immediate reproducibility.

- Slight Underperformance on DMS Stability Data: Slightly lags behind newer masked structure-based models in this specific setting.

- How does PoET-2 perform in real-world protein engineering campaigns compared to baseline PLMs?

summary.value: This paper introduces PoET-2, a multimodal and retrieval-augmented protein foundation model that combines sequence and structure information. By using homologous proteins as prompts, it enables context modeling without requiring multiple sequence alignment (MSA). PoET-2 uses a hierarchical Transformer encoder and two decoders, supporting both autoregressive generation and masked language modeling. Experiments show that PoET-2 achieves state-of-the-art zero-shot performance on insertion and deletion (indel) prediction in the ProteinGym benchmark, and performs significantly better than existing methods on higher-order mutations and clinical variant prediction tasks.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
**Strengths:**

- Lightweight and efficient: PoET-2 uses only 180 million parameters but achieves performance comparable to models with hundreds of millions or even trillions of parameters. It is fast and easy to deploy.
- Supports complex mutation prediction: PoET-2 is one of the few protein language models that can accurately predict the effects of insertions and deletions (indels), making it suitable for a wider range of mutation types.
- Highly data-efficient: In supervised learning, it only needs about 1/30 of the training data to outperform strong baselines like Kermut, which is especially useful in data-scarce scenarios.

**Weaknesses:**

- VenusREM performs much better than PoET-2 on substitution tasks. Although combining the two models helps, this does not mean PoET-2 alone is comparable to VenusREM. Also, VenusREM is only half the size of PoET-2 and can also handle structural inputs. Its only weakness is handling indels. Overall, VenusREM still appears to be a stronger tool for protein engineering.

questions.value:
1. Since the pairwise distances between backbone atoms are already given, the position of each $C_{\alpha}$ atom is mostly determined. Is the additional local distance feature $x_{atomb}$ really necessary? Is there any ablation study to show its impact?

2. For the retrieval step, the model only uses AlphaFoldDB structures corresponding to the query sequences. These predicted structures may be low-quality in some cases. Could the authors consider using a template search strategy, similar to AlphaFold's, to improve retrieval quality?

3. Although the paper shows that combining PoET-2 with VenusREM improves overall performance, Table 1 indicates that VenusREM consistently outperforms PoET-2 on substitution tasks. Ignoring indels, doesn’t this suggest that VenusREM is already a stronger model for typical protein engineering tasks?
   In addition, VenusREM is only half the size of PoET-2 (110M vs. 182M) and also supports structural inputs. Other than its lack of indel prediction, its capabilities are mostly similar. Since most real-world tasks focus on substitutions, how do the authors view the overall advantages of PoET-2 compared to VenusREM? Are there specific settings where PoET-2 clearly outperforms VenusREM on its own, without relying on model ensembling?

final_justification.value: I acknowledge the authors’ clarification regarding the use of ensembling and the additional analysis of PoET-2’s performance in specific scenarios. However, I believe the primary performance improvement comes from combining PoET-2 with VenusREM, which addresses a relatively narrow complementarity rather than showing a fundamentally novel or broadly impactful contribution from PoET-2 alone. While the indel prediction ability is a valuable addition, it remains unclear whether PoET-2 alone offers sufficient advantage for the majority of real-world protein engineering tasks focused on substitutions. Therefore, I will maintain my original score.

summary.value: The paper proposes PoET-2 – a multimodal foundation model achieving state-of-the-art results on standard protein fitness prediction benchmarks. Additionally, PoET-2 enables addressing previously unsolvable tasks with PLMs, such as indel mutations. The method introduces several new components, which are well-justified by ablation studies and thus provide a valuable contribution for future research in the field.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
Strengths

- Strong empirical results across several standard protein fitness prediction benchmarks (e.g., ProteinGym mutational scanning and clinical datasets).
- PoET-2 enables zero-shot indel and higher-order variant effect prediction, which were either not addressable or achieved only limited performance in prior methods.
- The proposed method is technically solid and well justified through extensive ablation experiments presented in the supplemental information.
- The method is shown to be both parameter- and data-efficient.

Weaknesses

- Without ensambling, PoET-2 underperforms VenusREM on the most well-established DMS substitutions benchmark. While, this is a minor issue considering that the authors demonstrate PoET-2 can be effectively ensembled with VenusREM, it would be great if the authors could provide more detailed comparison of the methods or more detailed discussions on the differences in their performance.
- Section 3 of the main text mainly discusses well-established machine learning components (e.g., “autoregressive decoder”, PLM and CLM losses) or technical details (e.g., binning of distances between alpha carbons), but omits seemingly important model components described in B.5 (e.g., 3Di token tracks). Could the authors revise Section 3 to make the method description more concise and complete?
- Figure 1 lacks a caption and is not straightforward to understand without one. For example, what exactly are the outputs of PoET-2?

Minor comments

- The phrase "protein function" in the title may be confusing, as the paper primarily focuses on protein fitness prediction. Protein function typically refers to tasks like enzyme EC number prediction, which are not directly addressed in this paper.
- The title, abstract, and introduction mention “retrieval-augmented,” but afterwards this concept is only mentioned in the discussion and not in the methods section. Please clarify what is meant by “retrieval-augmented.” Does it refer to the model’s ability to retrieve MSA sequences given a query sequences?
- Please discuss VenusREM in related work and describe the ensembling procedure.
- Lines 130–132. This statement does not appear to be supported by the experiments.
- Line 154. It is unclear how D is used in the model.
- The paper lacks the discussion of future work.

questions.value:
- Both PoET-2 and VenusREM leverage sequence, structure, and MSA-derived homolog information. Could the authors comment on why PoET-2 may underperform VenusREM on the DMS substitutions benchmark?
- Could the authors present additional experiments demonstrating, for example, the generative capabilities of the model, in addition to zero-shot or supervised fitness prediction benchmarks?

summary.value: This paper presents PoET-2, a multimodal, retrieval-augmented protein language model designed to improve protein variant effect prediction. Unlike prior PLMs, PoET-2 integrates both sequence and structure information through a hierarchical encoder and dual decoders optimized for both causal and masked language modeling. It can ingest evolutionary homologs and optionally structural templates to inform its predictions. The model shows strong performance on tasks involving indels and higher-order mutations, surpassing or matching state-of-the-art methods such as VenusREM and PoET-1, especially when ensembling is applied. PoET-2 also demonstrates strong generalization in supervised learning settings, particularly with limited training data, highlighting its utility in practical protein engineering applications.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
Strengths
- PoET-2 introduces a flexible architecture that incorporates homologous sequences and structures as context for language modeling, enabling more informed and family-specific variant predictions.

- The model is particularly effective for predicting the effects of indels and higher-order mutations, addressing a known limitation in many existing PLMs.

Weakness
- In the key evaluation benchmark (zero-shot DMS substitution), PoET-2 underperforms VenusREM on the main metric (Spearman correlation). While PoET-2 outperforms other baselines, its results are reported as ensemble averages over multiple prompts and context lengths, whereas baselines are not ensembled. It is unclear how much of the performance gain is attributable to architectural advantages versus ensembling.

- The model relies heavily on retrieval of homologous sequences or structures, which may not be available for orphan proteins or rapidly evolving families such as antibodies. The model’s performance on proteins with rare homologs should be reported.

- The paper does not provide a clear conclusion on which application scenarios PoET-2 is best suited for. Its performance is mixed--PoET-2 is better at predicting the mutation effect of indels but not substitution, excelling in indel and higher-order mutation prediction but lagging in single-substitution prediction. The practical implications of these trade-offs should be better discussed.

questions.value:
- Why did you choose embeddings from the MLM decoder and LLRs from the CLM decoder? Have you tested alternative configurations such as using embeddings and LLRs from both decoders or swapping their roles?

- Figure 2 shows performance trends with decreasing training data size, but no error bars or standard deviations. Given the performance for small sample sizes (e.g., 10 examples) could be unstable on different draws of training data, can you report the variance across multiple runs?

- Please report PoET-2’s performance without the length reweighting adjustment for indel variants to better understand its importance.

final_justification.value: During the discussion, the authors acknowledged that a weakness I noted in my original review was a limitation of their work -- the proposed method only outperformed existing methods in mutation effect prediction for insertions/deletions as a standalone method; but for substitution effect prediction, the proposed method is not performant and needs to be ensembled with existing methods for enhanced performance. This limitation substantially weakened the significance of this work. From this point of view, while the authors' response addressed most of my questions, it did not strengthen the significance of this work. With that said, considering the improved prediction for indels could be a contribution to the literature, I raised my score from 3 to 4.

title.value: Understanding protein function with a multimodal retrieval-augmented foundation model

abstract.value: Protein language models (PLMs) learn probability distributions over natural protein sequences. By learning from hundreds of millions of natural protein sequences, protein understanding and design capabilities emerge. Recent works have shown that scaling these models improves structure prediction, but does not seem to improve mutation understanding and representation quality for protein function prediction. We introduce PoET-2, a multimodal, retrieval-augmented protein foundation model that incorporates in-context learning of family-specific evolutionary constraints with optional structure conditioning to learn generative distributions over protein sequences. PoET-2 uses a hierarchical transformer encoder that is equivariant to sequence context ordering and a dual decoder architecture with both causal and masked language modeling objectives, allowing PoET-2 to operate in both fully generative and bidirectional representation learning modes. PoET-2 achieves state-of-the-art performance on zero-shot variant effect prediction, excelling at scoring variants with multiple mutations and challenging indel mutations. In supervised settings, PoET-2 embeddings outperform previous methods for learning sequence-function relationships, especially with small datasets. This work highlights the benefits of combining retrieval augmentation with multimodal, family-centric modeling for advancing protein foundation models.
